newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam, U.S. seek to smooth over differences.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam, U.S. seek to smooth over differences.

text.p: The United States and Vietnam on Tuesday sought to smooth differences over the best way for the two former wartime foes to forge closer economic ties.

Speaking to reporters after meeting Communist Party Secretary General Do Muoi, Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said Muoi had repeated Hanoi's hope for quick progress on closer ties but also voiced understanding of the difficulties involved.

"He said that he hoped that we could move on various aspects of economic normalisation at a good pace," Rubin said after the 55-minute meeting. "But he also said that he understood...these involved complications."
Those complications include a commitment by Vietnam to more open markets and improved labour practices.

Washington and Hanoi differed publicly on Monday over the best way to move their relationship forward, after signing a landmark deal to reschedule debt run up by America's former Saigon ally during the Vietnam War.
Rubin on Monday stressed the importance of Vietnam's pressing ahead with economic reform, saying that was the way for it to win trade concessions and financing from Washington.
But Prime Minister Vo Van Kiet argued that Washington, not Hanoi, was responsible for the slow progress the two countries had made in normalising their economic relationship.
"Vietnam seriously recognises that the reason for that is not caused by the Vietnamese side," Kiet was quoted by the official Vietnam News Agency as saying.

The highest ranking U.S. economic official to visit since the war ended in 1975, Rubin said he had praised the Vietnamese peoples' work ethic during his meetings with officials, saying that was the key to the nation's ultimate economic success.
He also spoke briefly of the importance that the United States placed in democratic principles, but did not elaborate.
Earlier, Rubin told reporters he had not directly raised the issue of alleged human rights abuses in Vietnam during meetings on Monday with Kiet and Finance Minister Sinh Hung.

The issue, though, did come up indirectly when he discussed conditions that Vietnam would need to meet to win trade concessions and financing from the United States, such as the improvement of labour practices.

The signing of the $145 million debt rescheduling accord on Monday cleared one hurdle to broader economic ties. The next, more daunting task is to seal a trade accord. Negotiations on that front are scheduled to resume in Hanoi later this month.

A trade deal is one condition needed for Vietnam to earn Most Favoured Nation (MFN) trading status. MFN, which guarantees non-discriminatry tarriffs on goods shipped into America, would give Vietnam access to the world's largest consumer market.

Speaking to college students before his meeting with Muoi, Rubin promised to do what he could to speed up economic normalisation, but repeated an earlier warning that Hanoi needed to do more to earn U.S. assistance.
"I"m going to see if I can help," he said. "But these things take time."
He also promised to work on a Vietnamese request for treasury help in improving its battered banking and financial services industries.
